title: Understanding the Gift Card Fallacy
subtitle: how we can share the pie without shrinking it

lines.text: Almost every argument about the economy comes down to the same tug of war.
On one side: grow the pie. Make the economy as big and productive as it can be.
On the other: share the pie. Make sure the slices aren't wildly unequal.
Most people assume you have to trade one for the other. This video is about why you don't.
First, why care about sharing at all? Because a dollar means more to someone who has fewer of them.
A hundred dollars is a week of groceries for a struggling family. For a billionaire, it's a rounding error.
A good rule of thumb: every time you double your money, you get about the same bump in happiness, whether you go from a thousand dollars to two thousand, or from a million to two million.
So take Alice and Bob, with five thousand dollars each. Now give Bob one thousand and Alice nineteen thousand. Twice the money, and less total happiness.
The Schöntrup index scores a whole society this way: the average logarithm of everyone's income. It rewards growing the pie and sharing it at the same time.
lines.say: The Shurn-troop index scores a whole society this way: the average logarithm of everyone's income. It rewards growing the pie and sharing it at the same time.

lines.text: Now, the cost of sharing. Economists call it deadweight loss, and the easiest way to see it is a gift.
Say I buy you a sweater for ten dollars. But you'd only pay seven dollars for it yourself.
I'm down ten dollars. You're up a sweater that's worth seven dollars to you.
That's three dollars of value that just disappeared. Nobody received it.
If I'd handed you a ten-dollar bill instead, you'd be up ten, and nothing would be lost. That missing three dollars is deadweight loss: value that could have existed, and doesn't.
Here's why that matters so much. When two people trade voluntarily, both expect to come out ahead, or they'd walk away.

A change that helps someone and hurts no one is called a Pareto improvement. It's the one kind of change we can know for sure makes the world better, without weighing one person's happiness against another's.
Say Dana would fix your roof for twenty dollars an hour, and you'd gladly pay twenty-five. The job happens, and five dollars of value is created between you.
Now put an eight-dollar tax on that hour of work. Dana needs twenty-eight to make it worth her while, and you'll only pay twenty-five. The job never happens.
The government collects nothing. Dana loses the work, your roof still leaks, and five dollars of value never comes into existence. That's the deadweight loss of taxing a trade.
A tax on trading is like a speeding ticket for mutually beneficial interactions.

So here's the first rule of efficient policy. A Pareto improvement makes the world better by definition, so a tax that stops one from happening makes the world worse by definition. Don't get in the way of useful trades.
Now look at how we usually try to share the pie.
Steep income tax brackets tax the trade of your work for pay, and tax it harder the more of it you do.
Minimum wages and rent control are price controls. They block some trades outright, and they hide a tax inside.

Take an apartment worth three thousand dollars a month, rent-controlled at two thousand. That's the same as giving the tenant a thousand-dollar rent voucher, paid for by a thousand-dollar tax on one landlord who happened to own that building. Why that landlord, instead of everyone?
So the debate becomes a gamble. Share more, and the pie shrinks. Will bigger slices for the poor make up for a smaller pie? Maybe. Maybe not.
But there's a mistake hiding inside that whole framing. Call it the gift card fallacy.

Look at the safety net. Food stamps: a grocery gift card. Housing vouchers: a rent gift card. Free public parking: a gift card for drivers, paid for by everyone. Even the public library is a gift card for books.
Every one of them is the sweater. A family that needs a winter coat more than groceries can't make that trade. The gap between what the benefit cost and what it's worth to them simply vanishes.

The usual defense is that officials know better what people need. But a bureaucrat can't see inside your life, and answers to politics, not to you. The people who know what a struggling family needs most are that family.
There are real exceptions. Things nobody can be fenced out of, like national defense, have to be funded directly. Nearly everything else? Cash.
Here's the good news. Economics already has a theorem for this: the second welfare theorem.

It says you can pick whatever amount of sharing you want, a little or a lot, and get there without shrinking the pie. Move money with transfers that don't depend on any trade, then let markets handle the rest.
That splits one fight into two separate questions. How much to share is a question of values. How to share it is a question of engineering, and engineering has better and worse answers.
So where does the money come from? Start with taxes that don't block useful trades.

Pollution first. When a factory dumps smoke on its neighbors for free, it produces too much, because someone else is paying part of the bill. A pollution tax charges that cost back to the polluter. It actually grows the pie.
Next, land. Picture an empty lot. A train station opens nearby. Then shops, then a hospital, then thousands of neighbors. The lot is suddenly worth far more.
The owner didn't do any of that. The lot soaked up its value from everything around it.

So a tax on land value falls on value the owner didn't create. The bill doesn't change based on anything they do: whether they work, build, sell, or trade. The person paying the tax isn't the person who made the value, so no trade gets blocked, and there's no deadweight loss.

Need more than that? Only then start taxing trades, beginning with the least harmful. First, a flat tax on consumption, which doesn't punish saving and investing. Income taxes come dead last. And keep each one to a single flat rate, so no bracket punishes a good year.
Then split the money equally. Every citizen gets the same check.

Try a forty percent flat rate with a ten thousand dollar dividend. Earn twelve thousand, and you take home seventeen thousand two hundred. Earn a million, and you pay thirty-nine percent. As progressive as any bracket system, with no brackets at all.
And because the check never shrinks when you earn more, there's no welfare cliff. Every extra hour of work leaves you better off.
So stop treating how much to share and how to share as the same argument. Whatever amount you choose, cash delivers it cheaper.
The poor end up with more. Taxpayers pay less. At the same time.
A free-market welfare state. Just give people money.
